title: Waterspout Beside Your Boat in the Dark: What Now?
logline: Sailing solo at night south of Bermuda with a dead radio, you watch a dark spot on the sea grow into a waterspout. Your instinct to run straight away fails. Only turning across its path saves you.
essence: Alone at night, you outlast a waterspout by fighting the instinct to flee and crossing its path.

hero.name: Mateo
hero.description: Solo sailor in his thirties on a 9 m sloop, oilskins and headlamp, steering by hand at night south of Bermuda.
hero.flaw: Curious and stubborn: he looks closer first, then flees in a straight line; his VHF radio is dead, so nobody can help.

hook.visual: Frame 0: Mateo at the tiller, eyes wide in fear, warm cabin lamp on his face; a moonlit funnel looms behind him; camera already pushing in through blown spray.

core_question.text: How do you survive a waterspout next to your boat at night?

stakes.physical: Violent winds and flying gear can capsize the sloop or throw Mateo overboard.
stakes.legal_ethical: With a dead radio he cannot warn other boats or call for help; his own seamanship decides everything.
stakes.mortal: Alone at night in open water, going overboard or capsizing means he likely never gets home.

spine.once_upon_a_time: Once upon a time a solo sailor crossed the night sea south of Bermuda.
spine.every_day: Every day he trusted his instincts and his radio.
spine.one_day: One day his radio died and a dark spot began spinning behind his boat.
because_of_that: Because of that, he ran straight away, and the funnel kept closing.
Because of that, he stopped, judged its drift against the mast, and saw it slide across his bow.
Because of that, he fought his instinct and turned ninety degrees across its path.
spine.until_finally: Until finally the funnel passed astern and broke apart into rain.
spine.ever_since: Ever since then, he reads the water before he trusts his gut.

beats.name: CONTEXT

beats.name: ESCALATION_1

beats.name: MIDPOINT

beats.name: ESCALATION_2

narration.text: A dark waterspout is spinning beside your boat.
narration.adds: Names the threat and makes the viewer the sailor.

narration.text: Earlier. You sail alone, south of Bermuda.
narration.adds: Time jump back and location: the waters of the Bermuda Triangle.

narration.text: Your radio is dead. You're on your own.
narration.adds: No help can come; the flaw and limitation.

narration.text: But that dark spot behind you is spinning.
narration.adds: Tells the viewer the spot is a forming vortex, not a shadow.

narration.text: Your instinct says run straight away from it.
narration.adds: The gut reaction that motivates his straight-line run.

narration.text: Then the gap stops growing, and it drifts closer.
narration.adds: The run is not working; distance is the real clock.

narration.text: Worse, a spray ring now circles its base.
narration.adds: Names the spray ring as a named stage of a strengthening waterspout.

narration.text: Stay with me. Its next move changes everything.
narration.adds: Opens a loop: watch where it moves next.

narration.text: But this one grew up from the sea, not down.
narration.adds: Fair-weather spouts build from the water surface upward, unlike tornadoes.

narration.text: Step one: never steer closer, because curiosity closes the gap.
narration.adds: Official NWS rule: never approach to investigate.

narration.text: Step two: watch its drift against the mast. Then you know its path.
narration.adds: How to read its apparent motion before choosing a heading.

narration.text: But it slides left, straight across your bow.
narration.adds: Its direction makes his current heading the worst place to be.

narration.text: Breathe, because your hands want to panic.
narration.adds: His inner fight against panic, invisible from outside.

narration.text: Salt stings your eyes, and only seconds remain.
narration.adds: Sensation plus the shrinking time he has to act.

narration.text: But running away failed. You need the opposite instinct.
narration.adds: Judges the first attempt after the evidence and sets up the counter-intuitive step.

narration.text: Step three: turn ninety degrees to its path, so it misses you.
narration.adds: The NWS answer: cross its track at a right angle instead of fleeing along it.

narration.text: But no curse did this. You read the weather.
narration.adds: NOAA finds no evidence the Triangle is special; skill, not luck, decided it.

narration.text: Then a new dark spot spins—
narration.adds: Re-opens the danger and loops back to frame 0.

steps.instruction: Watch its drift against the mast.
Turn ninety degrees to its path.
steps.because: So it misses you instead of following your line.

facts.claim: NWS advises moving at a 90-degree angle to a waterspout's apparent motion and never moving closer to investigate.
facts.source_title: Waterspouts - National Weather Service Key West

facts.claim: Fair-weather waterspouts develop on the surface of the water and work their way upward; tornadic waterspouts form downward from thunderstorms.
facts.source_title: What is a waterspout? - NOAA National Ocean Service

facts.claim: Waterspouts develop through stages including a dark spot on the water, a spiral pattern, a spray ring, a mature vortex and decay.
facts.source_title: Waterspouts - National Weather Service Key West

facts.claim: NOAA says there is no evidence that disappearances occur more frequently in the Bermuda Triangle than in any other large, well-traveled area of ocean.
facts.source_title: Is there really a Bermuda Triangle? - NOAA National Ocean Service

overrides.reason: 156 words for 67 s is below the 90-95% voiced budget because CAN-N2 caps voiced speech at 80% to pay for reaction and key-sound gaps.
Only sourced numbers are spoken (ninety, step ordinals); the on-screen distance badge carries the countable clock, so we avoid inventing unsourced figures.
The tail after the answer holds the required relief beat (>= 1.5 s after peak), the NOAA Bermuda fact and the frame-match loop; it runs about 7.8 s instead of 4 s.
